title: Second Epilogue — Chapter 6
paragraphs: Only the expression of God's will, which is independent of time, can relate to a whole series of events spanning years or centuries, and only God, independent of everything, can by His will alone determine the direction of humanity's movement. But a human being acts in time and is himself part of events.

Restoring the first condition that was left out—the element of time—we see that no command can be carried out unless some prior command has already been given that makes the execution of the latest one possible.

No command ever appears out of nowhere or covers an entire series of events by itself; each command follows from another, and each always relates to one specific moment of an event, never to a whole series.

When we say, for instance, that Napoleon ordered armies to go to war, we are combining in one simultaneous expression a whole series of consecutive commands that depended on one another. Napoleon could not have commanded an invasion of Russia and never did so. One day he ordered certain papers to be written to Vienna, to Berlin, and to Petersburg; the next day he ordered certain decrees and instructions to the army, the fleet, and the commissariat, and so on and so on—millions of commands making up a series of commands corresponding to a series of events that brought the French army to Russia.

If throughout his reign Napoleon issued commands about an invasion of England—spending more time and effort on that project than on any other—yet during his whole reign never once attempted it, and instead invaded Russia, with which he considered it advantageous to be allied, this was because the first set of commands did not and could not correspond to the course of events, while the second set did.

For an order to be reliably carried out, a person must command what can actually be done. But knowing what can and what cannot be done is impossible—not only in the case of Napoleon's invasion of Russia, where millions of people participated, but even in the simplest event—because in either case millions of obstacles may arise.

Our mistaken belief that an event is caused by the command that precedes it comes from the fact that, after the event has taken place, out of thousands of commands only those few that happened to match the event are remembered as having been carried out. We forget about the others because they didn't match the event and therefore weren't executed.

We say that Napoleon wanted to invade Russia and invaded it. In reality, throughout Napoleon's entire career we never find anything resembling an expression of that desire. What we find is a series of commands—expressions of his will—that are enormously varied and vaguely directed. Out of Napoleon's countless series of unexecuted orders, one series—for the campaign of 1812—was carried out, not because those particular orders differed in any way from the ones that weren't, but because they happened to coincide with the course of events that led the French army into Russia. Just as a stencil doesn't produce the image on a wall because paint was applied from this side or that, but because paint was applied from all sides of the stencil's cut-out shape.
So, examining the relationship between commands and events in time, we find that a command can never be the cause of an event, but that a definite interdependence exists between the two.

To understand what this interdependence consists of, it is necessary to restore another condition that was left out of every command—a condition that applies to commands issued by human beings, not by God: the person who gives the command is himself a participant in the event.
This relationship of the commander to those he commands is precisely what is called power. This relationship consists in the following:

For collective action, people always combine into certain groups, and in these groups—regardless of the differences in the goals set for the collective action—the relationship between participants is always the same.

People who unite in these groups always relate to one another in such a way that the greater number take a more direct part, and the smaller number take a less direct part, in the collective action they have joined together to perform.
Of all the groups in which people combine for collective action, one of the most clear-cut and well-defined examples is an army.

Every army is made up of the lowest ranks—the ordinary soldiers—of whom there are always the most; of the next higher rank—corporals and non-commissioned officers, of whom there are fewer; of still higher officers, of whom there are fewer yet; and so on up to the highest military command, which is concentrated in a single person.

A military organization can be precisely compared to a cone, whose base—the widest part—consists of the rank and file; the next section, narrower and higher, consists of the next grades of the army; and so on to the apex of the cone, which represents the commander-in-chief.

The soldiers, who are the most numerous, form the lowest section and the base of the cone. The ordinary soldier does the actual fighting—the stabbing, hacking, burning, and looting—and always receives his orders from those above him; he never gives orders himself. The non-commissioned officers (of whom there are fewer) less often perform the actual fighting than the soldiers, but they do give orders. An officer still more rarely takes direct part in the action, and gives orders more frequently. A general does nothing but command troops, indicate the objective, and hardly ever uses a weapon himself. The commander-in-chief never takes direct part in the action at all, and only makes general plans for the movement of the masses. A similar relationship exists among people who combine for any kind of collective action—in commerce, in government, in every human enterprise.

And so, without analyzing in detail every section of the cone and every rank and position in any administrative or public enterprise from the lowest to the highest, we see a law by which people combine to take collective action in relationships such that the more directly they participate in carrying out the action, the less they can direct it, and the more they direct, the less they directly participate. The proportion rises from the soldiers at the base of the cone to its single apex—the supreme commander, who takes the least direct part in the action and devotes his activity primarily to commanding.
This relationship of the people who command to those who carry out the commands is what constitutes the essence of the concept called power.

Having restored the condition of time—under which all events occur—we find that a command is only carried out when it corresponds to an actual series of events. Restoring the essential condition of the relationship between those who command and those who execute, we find that by the very nature of the case, those who command take the least direct part in the event itself, and that their activity is devoted exclusively to commanding.
